extracted_notes.text: The main drivers of population growth are immigration and, to a lesser extent, natural growth.
Canada has one of the highest per-capita immigration rates in the world, driven mainly by economic policy and family reunification.
A record 483,390 immigrants were admitted in 2024.
Canada leads the world in refugee resettlement; it resettled more than 47,600 in 2022.
New immigrants settle mostly in major urban areas, such as Toronto, Montreal, and Vancouver.

Canada's population density, at 4.2 inhabitants per square kilometre (11/sq mi), is among the lowest in the world, with approximately 95 percent of the population residing south of the 55th parallel north.
Canada is highly urbanized, with over 80 percent of the population living in urban centres.
The most densely populated part of the country is the Quebec City-Windsor Corridor in Southern Quebec and Southern Ontario along the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River.
The majority of Canadians (81.1 percent) live in family households, 12.1 percent report living alone, and 6.8 percent live with other relatives or unrelated persons.

Fifty-one percent of households are couples with or without children, 8.7 percent are single-parent households, 2.9 percent are multigenerational households, and 29.3 percent are single-person households.

The major panethnic groups chosen were: European (52.5 percent), North American (22.9 percent), Asian (19.3 percent), North American Indigenous (6.1 percent), African (3.8 percent), Latin, Central and South American (2.5 percent), Caribbean (2.1 percent), Oceanian (0.3 percent), and other (6 percent).

The country's ten largest self-reported ethnic or cultural origins in 2021 were Canadian (accounting for 15.6 percent of the population), followed by English (14.7 percent), Irish (12.1 percent), Scottish (12.1 percent), French (11.0 percent), German (8.1 percent), Chinese (4.7 percent), Italian (4.3 percent), Indian (3.7 percent), and Ukrainian (3.5 percent).

One out of every four Canadians or 26.5 percent of the population belonged to a non-White and non-Indigenous visible minority, the largest of which in 2021 were South Asian (2.6 million people; 7.1 percent), Chinese (1.7 million; 4.7 percent), Black (1.5 million; 4.3 percent), Filipinos (960,000 2.6 percent), Arabs (690,000; 1.9 percent), Latin Americans (580,000; 1.6 percent), Southeast Asians (390,000; 1.1 percent), West Asians (360,000; 1.0 percent), Koreans (220,000; 0.6 percent) and Japanese (99,000; 0.3 percent).

The 2021 census indicated that 8.3 million people, or almost one-quarter (23.0 percent) of the population, reported themselves as being or having been a landed immigrant or permanent resident in Canada--above the 1921 census previous record of 22.3 percent.

insight_badge_data.expanded_detail: The 2021 census revealed that 23.0 percent of the population were landed immigrants or permanent residents. This figure surpassed the previous historical record of 22.3 percent set in 1921.

blocks.text_content: Once they arrive, the vast majority of these new Canadians do not spread evenly across the landscape, but gravitate toward specific hubs of activity.

Canada is a highly urbanized nation, with over **80 percent** of its people living in urban centers. For new immigrants, the draw of major cities is almost irresistible, as they offer the infrastructure and communities needed to start anew.

itemized_breakdown_data.context_text: New immigrants to Canada primarily settle in the country's largest urban centers.

blocks.text_content: This concentration in cities is part of a larger geographic trend where the population is heavily skewed toward the southern border.

Despite its massive landmass, Canada's population is remarkably concentrated. A significant portion of the country remains sparsely populated, while the majority of residents are clustered in the south.

fact_grid_data.title: Canada's Urbanization
fact_grid_data.intro_text: Canada is characterized by a high level of urbanization, with a significant portion of its population concentrated in specific regions.

blocks.text_content: This geographic imbalance is most evident when looking at the 55th parallel north, which acts as a dividing line for the vast majority of the population.

The vast majority of Canadians live in the southern regions of the country, leaving the north largely open. Approximately **95 percent** of the population resides south of the **55th parallel north**.

percentage_display_data.context_text: A vast majority of Canada's population is concentrated in the southern regions of the country.

blocks.text_content: This extreme concentration in the south creates a paradox: while cities are crowded, the country as a whole remains one of the most sparsely populated places on Earth.

When averaged across its entire territory, Canada's population density is among the lowest in the world. This creates a unique relationship between the people and the vast, often harsh, wilderness that surrounds them.

insight_badge_data.expanded_detail: Canada has a population density of 4.2 inhabitants per square kilometre, making it one of the lowest in the world.

blocks.text_content: While the geography of the nation is sparse, the internal geography of the Canadian home is defined by a variety of living arrangements.
The way Canadians live is varied. While the majority reside in family-based settings, a significant number of people live alone or in non-traditional arrangements.

percentage_display_data.title: Population Distribution by Household Type
percentage_display_data.context_text: The majority of Canadians reside in family households, while a smaller portion live alone or with other relatives and unrelated persons.

blocks.text_content: Looking closer at the 2021 census, we can see a more detailed breakdown of who exactly makes up these households.
Household structures in Canada range from couples and single parents to multigenerational homes. These arrangements reflect the diverse social and economic realities of the population.

blocks.text_content: Beyond the structure of the home, the identity of the people within them is defined by a rich, multicultural tapestry.

Canada is one of the most ethnically diverse nations in the world. The 2021 census identified several major panethnic groups that contribute to this multicultural identity, ranging from European and North American to Asian and Indigenous origins.

entity_profiles_data.title: Canada: Major Panethnic Groups
entity_profiles_data.intro_text: The 2021 Canadian census identified several major panethnic groups that contribute to the country's multicultural identity.

blocks.text_content: While panethnic groups provide a broad overview, many Canadians identify with more specific cultural or ethnic origins.
When asked about their heritage, Canadians report a wide array of origins. The ten largest groups include a mix of traditional colonial roots and more recent immigrant populations.

blocks.text_content: This diversity is further highlighted by the presence of a significant visible minority population, which has grown substantially over the last several decades.

The proportion of the population belonging to a non-White and non-Indigenous visible minority has grown significantly. By 2021, one out of every four Canadians belonged to such a group, reflecting the country's evolving demographic shift.
